name: Postclassic Maya states
summary: Maya kingdoms after the Classic collapse: Chichén Itzá and Mayapan in Yucatán, the K’iche’ and Kaqchikel in highland Guatemala, and the Itza of Nojpetén, the last independent Maya kingdom, conquered by Spain in 1697.

knownFor.label: Dresden Codex
knownFor.note: One of four surviving Maya books.

location.value: The Yucatán peninsula, the highlands of Guatemala and the Petén lakes, in today’s Mexico, Guatemala and Belize.

climate.value: Tropical: hot all year, with a summer rainy season; the north of Yucatán is drier, and the highlands are cooler.

resources.value: Maize farmland, cacao in wetter lowlands, salt from the Yucatán coast, cotton, honey, and obsidian and jade from the highlands.

disasters.value: Droughts, hurricanes and locust plagues; Maya chronicles remember famines in Yucatán in the 1400s.

population.value: Mayapan itself had an estimated 15,000–17,000 people. The page gives no regional total.

urbanisation.value: Towns rather than giant cities: Mayapan had perhaps 15,000 people; Q’umarkaj and Iximche were highland capitals.

disease.value: Smallpox and other European diseases spread ahead of the Spanish around 1520, killing many people.

migration.value: Groups linked to the Itza and to Gulf Coast peoples probably moved into Yucatán; the Itza later settled in Petén.

economicBase.value: Mayapan was an import and export centre trading luxury goods such as cotton, salt and honey, reaching Honduras, Belize and Cozumel, with obsidian from El Chayal in Guatemala.

tradeRoutes.value: Canoe trade around the coast of Yucatán via Cozumel and Xicalango; Columbus met a Maya trading canoe in 1502.

wealth.value: Wealth came from cacao, salt, cotton cloth and slaves traded along the coast and to central Mexico.

moneyAndTax.value: Cacao beans, cotton cloth and copper bells were used as money; subjects paid tribute in goods and labour.

inequality.value: Mostly small-scale societies; some ranked chiefs and families.

governmentType.value: Mayapan was the political and cultural capital of Yucatán from the 1220s to the 1440s, under a Cocom-led council that lasted over 200 years. The K'iche' kingdoms are not on this page.

keyRulers.value: The page names no K'iq'ab or Kan Ek' kings.

succession.value: Rule passed within noble lineages, such as the Cocom of Mayapan and the Kaweq of the K’iche’; councils chose among heirs.

institutions.value: Councils of lords, town rulers (batabs) and a paramount lord (halach uinic) in Yucatán; priests ran temples and calendars.

eliteConflict.value: Lineage rivalry: the Xiu revolt destroyed Mayapan (about 1441), and the Kaqchikel broke from the K’iche’ in the 1400s.

armyAndTech.value: Warriors with spears, bows, atlatls (spear throwers), shields and quilted cotton armour; towns had walls.

majorWars.value: Mayapan was abandoned around 1448; the Kʼicheʼ capital Qʼumarkaj fell to Alvarado in 1524.

territoryChange.value: Split into many small provinces after Mayapan fell; Spain conquered the highlands (1524), Yucatán (1546) and Nojpetén (1697).

alliancesRivals.value: The Kaqchikel first helped the Spanish against their K’iche’ rivals (1524), then rebelled against Spain.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; skilled local technologies.

openness.value: Open to trade and ideas from central Mexico, Honduras and the Gulf Coast through traders and canoe routes.

communicationTransport.value: Canoes along coasts and rivers, raised roads (sacbeob) in Yucatán, and porters on foot, as there were no pack animals.

religion.value: The Temple of Kukulcan is Mayapan's main temple, and Kukulcan is said to have founded the site after the fall of Chichen Itza. Chaak and Ix Chel are not mentioned.

languageWriting.value: Yucatec, K’iche’, Kaqchikel and other Maya languages; hieroglyphic books such as the Dresden Codex were still made.

artsArchitecture.value: Chichén Itzá’s Castillo pyramid, the walled town of Mayapan, and murals at Tulum and Santa Rita Corozal.

socialStructure.value: Ruling lords and nobles, priests, merchants and warriors, commoner farmers, and slaves taken in war or for debt.

sharedIdentity.value: Identity rested on each people, village and language rather than one state.

dailyLife.value: Families ate maize as tortillas and tamales, with beans, squash and chilli; nobles drank chocolate; houses were of poles and thatch.

neighbours.value: Aztec and Gulf Coast traders to the north-west, Central American peoples to the south-east, and from 1500s the Spanish.

ideasReligions.value: The Maya calendar and astronomy continued, along with Mexican ideas such as the cult of the feathered serpent.

colonisation.value: Spain conquered the highland kingdoms from 1524 and Yucatán by 1546; the Itza held out until 1697.

riseSignals.value: Early Postclassic AD 950–1200, Late Postclassic AD 1200–1539; Chichen Itza rose and then declined dramatically in the 11th century.

peakPeriod.value: Mayapan was Yucatán's capital from the 1220s to the 1440s.

declineSignals.value: The fall of Mayapan (about 1441), epidemics and the Spanish conquest from 1524 broke the Maya kingdoms.

outcome.value: The last independent Maya city, Nojpetén, fell to the Spanish in 1697.

overallCertainty.value: Known from archaeology, oral history and Spanish and later records; population figures are estimates.
